_comment: THE DECLARED REQUEST LIST. One row per case; adding a case is adding a row.
Fields: `id` (also the golden's filename), `phase`, `why`, `method`, `target`,
`principal` (a name from world.json, or null for no Authorization header),
`token_literal` (a credential that is not in the token file), `client_ip`
(null omits CF-Connecting-IP), `headers` (ordered pairs, duplicates allowed),
`body` ({text_lines|json|raw_text}), `raw_request` (literal request lines, for
the two cases whose request line cannot be expressed by an HTTP client at
all), `normalize` (declared licences to differ - see suite.py normalizations),
`body_kind` (`snapshot` records the extracted tree instead of the bytes),
`canary`, `negative_route`.
PHASE is `write` for a case that MAY CHANGE THE STORE, and `read` for every
case that cannot. cases.py refuses a `read` row placed after the first
`write` row: a successful write moves entry mtimes, and every report body
carries `entry-files=` and `newest=<mtime>`, so a read recorded afterwards
would depend on list order rather than on the declared world.
The If-Match literals below are the sha256 (first 16 hex) of the declared
entry bytes, SPELLED BY HAND. If world.json's text changes they stop
matching and the case answers 412 - loudly, in the diff, which is the
intended behaviour: the precondition is a contract with a caller and the
caller computes it from bytes it holds.

cases.why: the kubelet's probe. Unauthenticated by design, and it says nothing but `ok`.
the probe must not require a CF-Connecting-IP the kubelet has no reason to send: health is answered BEFORE the client-IP check.
HEAD carries the same headers and no body.
a valid credential buys NOTHING extra here - no version, no scope count, no revision.
a non-API path is the uniform 401, not a 404: a 404 would let an unauthenticated caller map the URL space.
one missing slash is not the API prefix. Answered 401 even to a VALID credential, because the prefix check precedes the token check.
the same, for the path an operator's instinct reaches for. It is also NOT counted as a failed auth - see the rate-limit note in server.py.
no Authorization header at all.
a credential that is not in the token file. Must be indistinguishable from every other refusal.
the peer is a trusted proxy and sent no CF-Connecting-IP: there is no bucket to meter, so the request FAILS CLOSED rather than sharing one key with everybody.
TWO CF-Connecting-IP headers. Which one is the client is unanswerable, so the request is refused rather than guessed at.
an unhandled method reaches send_error, which is overridden to answer the ONE uniform 401 rather than a 501 page that echoes the verb.
the same, for the verb that would otherwise echo the request.
an invented verb. It must look exactly like a bad token, and it must be METERED like one.
urlsplit RAISES on this target, and absolute-form is mandatory-to-accept - so a conforming client can send it. It must be a uniform 401, not an unhandled ValueError with no response at all.
cases.oracle_only_why: THE REQUEST LINE NEVER REACHES A HANDLER IN A SERVER WHOSE FRAMEWORK PARSES IT FIRST. `urlsplit` RAISES on this target, so the oracle has to catch it INSIDE its own handler and answer the uniform 401 - which is the contract this row was written to pin, and it is the oracle's to keep. Go's `net/http` rejects the request line in `readRequest`, before any handler exists to be reached, and answers its own 400. The SECURITY property survives intact on both: an unparseable target reveals nothing about the store, which is the same reasoning `raw-malformed-request-line` is already recorded under rather than called a defect. What is asserted for a port instead: NOTHING, and saying so is the point. The answer comes from the framework's own request parser, before a line of the port runs, so there is no code here to write a test against - the security property holds because a framed 400 mentions no scope, which is a property of that framework rather than one this repository can pin. That is the honest shape of this particular skip, and it is why the row's own `why` is kept above it.

cases.why: six bytes, before `self.path` exists. The answer is a bare HTTP/0.9 body with NO status line and NO headers, because parse_request never established a version - recorded as its own shape rather than faked into a 401.
cases.oracle_only_why: HTTP/0.9 IS A PROPERTY OF `http.server`, NOT A DESIGNED CONTRACT. `parse_request` never establishes a version for a six-byte request line, so `send_response_only` suppresses the status line and every header and the body arrives with no framing at all. That is the oracle's own shape and it is worth recording FOR THE ORACLE; no other implementation has a reason to reproduce it, and Go's `net/http` answers a framed 400. Already excluded from the uniform-401 set for the same reason.

cases.why: 🔴 THE ONE CASE THAT CAN SEE A MIS-FRAMED REPORT. Every other case is issued through an HTTP client, which reads EXACTLY Content-Length bytes - so comparing the two asks the client whether it agrees with itself, and a wrong length is invisible (measured: mutating the server to send len(body)-1 failed exactly ONE case). Asking for `Connection: close` makes the body readable to EOF, so its length is an independent observation. It is also why `report-content-length` may drop the header from a report's golden without dropping the claim.
the ordinary read. Two entries, newest first, with the scope's git HEAD in X-Store-Revision.
HEAD keeps every header and sends no body. Its Content-Length is normalized away for the same reason its GET's is - see the head_matches_get relation, which pins that the two agree.
a bare row is UNRESTRICTED, so it reads a scope no allowlist names. Reads from a legacy token are deliberately unchanged by the scoping migration.
alpha-notes EXISTS and this caller may not see it. The refused half of the pair.
a scope that has never existed, asked by the same caller. The absent half of the pair.
a directory that exists and holds no entry: `scope-empty`, which must never render like a store that could not be read.
every file in the scope is malformed: `scope-unreadable`, X-Store-Exit 3, on a 200. The state this whole design exists to keep separate from `nothing recorded yet`.
?ref= addresses one entry.
a ref that resolves to nothing inside a scope that does.
?mode= is one of digest|list|full.
the third mode, so the vocabulary is pinned rather than sampled.
an unknown mode is a caller error, and the caller is authenticated so it may be told what it sent.
?limit= and ?page= together, on a scope with exactly two entries so page 2 is the last.
a query parameter NEVER silently defaults: a typo is a 400, not the default value.
parseable and out of range.
a repeated parameter: the server reads the LAST value, and that choice is a contract a port must reproduce.
`%2e%2e` decodes to `..`, and a path component reaches the filesystem. Refused 400 on the charset, not on the two spellings somebody thought of.
the route table names an arity, and a request that does not match it does not dispatch.
the same from the other side. `len(parts) == arity` mutated to `>=` once survived 318 tests.
the prefix with nothing after it: an API path with no head at all.
a head with no row. Spelled with an underscore on purpose - that spelling defeated a regex-based route guard once.
the ordinary search.
HEAD on the second read route, paired with its GET the same way.
`q` is required. There is no default query.
present and whitespace-only, which is the shape a required parameter is most often lost as.
a query that matches nothing, with the threshold pinned so the miss is a property of the query and not of the default.
every remaining query parameter this route accepts, at once.
the float parameter's own refusal, which is a different code path from the int one.
`all_scopes=1` names no scope, so a per-scope refusal has nothing to refuse. It means ALL THE CALLER'S SCOPES because the INDEX is narrowed - this row is what pins that.
the refused half of the search pair.
the absent half of the search pair.
unrestricted scope on the search route too.
the whole store as a gzipped PAX tar. The goldens hold the EXTRACTED tree - paths, contents, and mtimes to sub-second precision - never the archive bytes.
HEAD on the snapshot route: every header, no archive.
the FOURTH enumeration channel. This route builds no index, so the allowlist is applied to the candidate directory list - without it a caller allowed one scope could download every scope's files.
unrestricted: the same member set the wide principal gets.
?scope= narrows the archive, and X-Store-Entries describes the same filtered set.
the refused half of the snapshot pair: a scope filter naming a scope this caller may not see.
the absent half of the snapshot pair.
?scope= reaches the filesystem, so it is charset-checked exactly like a path component.

the conditional sync: a validator that MATCHES is answered 304 with no body, no Content-Type and no Content-Length. The literal is sha256 of the UNCOMPRESSED tar this world produces for this principal, SPELLED BY HAND like the If-Match literals above - if world.json changes it stops matching and this case answers 200, loudly, in the diff.
a validator that does NOT match is answered the whole archive, with the current ETag on it. The half a 304-only corpus could not tell from a route that answers 304 to everything.
RFC 9110 13.1.2's `*` - any current representation. Pinned because it is the one conditional whose answer does not depend on the world's bytes, so it stays a 304 across every fixture change.

THE WIDE PRINCIPAL'S VALIDATOR, PRESENTED BY THE NARROW ONE - answered 200, because the tag digests the archive THIS caller gets and the two callers do not get the same archive. A validator keyed on anything store-wide would answer 304 here and hand a narrowed caller a cache it may not hold.

A CONDITIONAL REQUEST IS NOT A WAY PAST A REFUSAL. The `*` above is the one validator that always matches, and this row is still the 400 `snapshot-bad-scope` is: the charset check runs before the conditional is even read.
the snapshot route is not a second, weaker door.
`read-only` is a claim about THIS ROUTE. recall has no write verb and never will.
the snapshot route added a GET and no write verb: WRITE_ROUTES holds no row for it.
PATCH appears in no row, which is how it stays refused - not by a separate rejecter it could be re-bound away from.
the same for DELETE, on the noun that has content to lose.
`entry` is a WRITE head only. A GET at it is a 404 from the read table, not a 405.
a write verb at a non-API path still goes through authenticate-then-refuse, so it is metered like everything else.
a write attempt with no credential is an unauthorised request, not a wrong method - and it is charged as one.

json.text: an append with a bad credential

cases.why: the same, with a credential that is merely wrong.
authentication precedes the precondition ladder entirely.
a bare row has no identity, so there is no ACTOR to attribute a bullet to. 403, and it says which row shape fixes it.
the legacy refusal is on the write ROUTES, so PUT is refused for the same reason POST is - and BEFORE anything is created.

an optional precondition is no precondition: 428. ALSO THE CANARY - it is authenticated and it touches no store state, which is what makes it the one authorized case that can be re-issued after the write phase and still expect the same answer.
`it exists and is exactly this` and `it does not exist` are mutually exclusive. Refused, never resolved by picking one.
`*` is the one value that turns the guard off while looking like it is on.
a header that is present and names no entity-tag is not a precondition.
a LIST on If-None-Match would mean `overwrite unless it is one of these`, which is the lost update If-Match exists to refuse, spelled backwards.
a malformed body is a caller error, answered as one - and the parser's own sentence rides the response.
cases.oracle_only_why: THE PARENTHESISED SENTENCE IS CPython's `json` MODULE'S DIAGNOSTIC (`Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes: line 1 column 2 (char 1)`), and it is an artifact of that parser rather than a contract a port can honour without shipping a second JSON parser to reproduce its wording. The row stays asserted against the oracle because the sentence really does ride the response there. What a port must still get right - a 400, `X-Store-Status: bad-request`, the `bad request: body must be JSON (` prefix, and a connection that is not dropped - is pinned in the Go tests named in README.md, because that is where an implementation's own diagnostics belong.

cases.why: nesting is what once raised RecursionError - not a ValueError - inside json.loads, dropping the connection with no response and NO AUDIT LINE. This depth is shallow enough to parse; the shape is the point.
cases.oracle_only_why: SAME REASON AS `post-bullets-not-json`: the body quotes CPython's own `Expecting value: line 1 column 51 (char 50)`. The DEFECT this row exists for - a nested body raising an error type the handler did not name, dropping the connection with no response and no audit line - is implementation-specific too: it was a `RecursionError` out of `json.loads`, and a parser that returns an error instead of unwinding the stack cannot reproduce it. The Go side pins the answerable half (a 400, not a dropped connection) in its own tests.

cases.why: every appended bullet records the actor AND the session.
the session is caller-supplied correlation data, so it is charset-checked before it goes anywhere near a file.
whitespace is not text.
one character over BULLET_TEXT_MAX, which the client refuses locally from the SAME constant. The server's own refusal is the contract.
an `actor` key is accepted and DISCARDED. This row sends one at a scope the caller cannot reach, so the answer is the 404 - the point is that the key does not turn it into a 400.

json.text: an append to a scope I may not see

cases.why: the refused half of the append pair. A refusal that is distinguishable from an absence is an enumeration API on a write verb just as on a read.

json.text: an append to a scope I may not see

cases.why: the absent half of the append pair.
the refused half of the replace pair. Note the precondition is WRONG and the answer is still 404, because the target does not resolve at all for this caller.
the absent half of the replace pair.
a ref that resolves to no entry, inside a scope the caller CAN write. Same 404, deliberately.

json.text: an append to a file the loader rejects

cases.why: an entry the loader could not parse is not a writable target, and it answers the same 404 as an absence.

json.text: an append to a nameless scope

cases.why: a component that is a valid path segment and names nothing. On the append route it is a 404 (the allowlist answers first); on the create route the same shape is a 400 - see put-create-ref-normalizes-away.

the scope is allowed and the REF normalizes to nothing: a caller error with a defined remedy, so it is said rather than 404'd. The asymmetry with the row above is real and is recorded rather than smoothed over.

json.text: the sidecar drops its lease during a rollout.

cases.why: text that hashes equal to a bullet already on disk. NOT ONE BYTE is written, and the response echoes the STORED line - whose year-2000 date is fixture data and is therefore pinned literally, with no date normalization on this row.

json.text: the conformance suite appended this bullet.

cases.why: the real append. The rendered line is pinned byte for byte EXCEPT its date - including the `[cairn: wide-reader/conf-1]` trailer, which is the whole of the attribution guarantee: the actor comes from the token and the body has no way to reach it.

json.text: the conformance suite appended this bullet.

cases.why: THE IDEMPOTENCY CRITERION, as a relationship between two requests: the identical text under a DIFFERENT session answers `duplicate` and writes nothing, because content_hash covers neither the date, the actor nor the session.

text_lines: REPLACED by the conformance suite, through PUT with a correct If-Match.
- ops skill `manage-widget` - invoke it for restarts
- 2000-01-03: the lease renewal races the readiness gate.

cases.why: the whole-file replace. Its ETag is sha256 of the bytes THIS REQUEST sent, so it is deterministic and pinned literally - no normalization.

the lost-update refusal. The file is UNCHANGED and the CURRENT revision rides the response, because a client told only `no` cannot retry - and a client that cannot retry re-sends without the precondition.
a CORRECT precondition and bytes the loader would reject: 422, and nothing is written. Targets the one fixture entry no other write case changes, so its revision is the same for both spare-six rows.

text_lines: CREATED by the conformance suite, through PUT with If-None-Match: *.
- ops skill `manage-newcomer` - invoke it for restarts
- 2000-01-03: this entry did not exist until the suite created it.

cases.why: create-if-absent. 201, not 200 - it is the only way a client can tell a create that landed from a replace that did, since both carry an ETag.
412 with a DISTINCT status token: a caller told only `412` cannot tell `somebody moved it, re-sync` from `it is already there, you wanted a replace`, and one of those is an infinite retry.
the create half's validity gate. The name stays free, so nothing later in the corpus depends on it.

_comment: TWO PROPERTIES THAT ARE RELATIONSHIPS BETWEEN RESPONSES. No per-response
golden can hold either: each case has its own file, and each would keep
passing if one of them grew a distinguishing header, because whoever
regenerated would have recorded the divergence.

head_matches_get._why: a HEAD must report the Content-Length its GET would have sent. Both values are host-dependent in LENGTH, so neither can live in a golden - but they can be compared to each other in one run.
head_matches_get.name: recall
head_matches_get.head: recall-authorized-head
